notes.text: Acts xxii, 3, &c.; Acts xxvi, 9, &c.
Bound — By the connivance, if not authority, of the governor, under Aretas the king. See Acts ix, 14, 24.

And suddenly — When God suddenly and vehemently attacks a sinner, it is the highest act of mercy. So Saul, when his rage was come to the height, is taught not to breathe slaughter. And what was wanting in time to confirm him in his discipleship, is compensated by the inexpressible terror he sustained. By his also the suddenly constituted apostle was guarded against the grand snare into which novices are apt to fall.
He heard a voice — Severe, yet full of grace.
To kick against the goads — is a Syriac proverb, expressing an attempt that brings nothing but pain.
It shall be told thee — So God himself sends Saul to be taught by a man, as the angel does Cornelius, chap. x, 5. Admirable condescension! that the Lord deals with us by men, like ourselves.

The men — stood - Having risen before Saul; for they also fell to the ground, chap. xxvi, 14. It is probable they all journeyed on foot. Hearing the noise - But not an articulate voice. And seeing the light, but not Jesus himself, chap. xxvi, 13, &c.

And he was three days — An important season! So long he seems to have been in the pangs of the new birth. Without sight - By scales growing over his eyes, to intimate to him the blindness of the state he had been in, to impress him with a deeper sense of the almighty power of Christ, and to turn his thoughts inward, while he was less capable of conversing with outward objects. This was likewise a manifest token to others, of what had happened to him in his journey, and ought to have humbled and convinced those bigoted Jews, to whom he had been sent from the sanhedrim.
Behold he is praying — He was shown thus to Ananias.
A man called Ananias — His name also was revealed to Saul.
But he answered — How natural it is to reason against God.
All that call on thy name — That is, all Christians.
He is a chosen vessel to bear my name — That is, to testify of me. It is undeniable, that some men are unconditionally chosen or elected, to do some works for God

For I — Do thou as thou art commanded. I will take care of the rest; will show him - In fact, through the whole course of his ministry. How great things he must suffer - So far will he be now from persecuting others.
The Lord hath sent me — Ananias does not tell Saul all which Christ had said concerning him. It was not expedient that he should know yet to how great a dignity he was called.

glossa.text: *And Saul.* He returns to that which he had said above: *Saul was still laying waste the Church. Of threatenings,* etc. Terrifying with threats, he afflicted with slaughter those present: it is doubted whether he killed or scourged, or did both. *Breathing.* He breathes after the manner of fire, and not incited by another he himself set others on fire.

*And falling.* Terrified, he flees back to the ground, or as one adoring he falls upon his face.

*Why me,* etc. ((BEDA.)) He says not: Why dost thou persecute, etc., *as far as, As long as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me ((Matth. XXV))*.
*I am Jesus.* He calls himself not God nor the Son of God, but, Receive, he says, the weak things of my humility, and lay aside the scales of thy pride.

*Arise.* Work untiring as an ox, and be a teacher of the Church. In the law it is written: *Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn ((I Cor. IX))*.

*Enter in. ((RAB.))* About to enter the city he is terrified, lest he bring sorrow upon the saints; thereafter the Lord is bidden to enter, that he may learn the faith which he had assailed.

*And it shall be said.* An example of learning is given, and pride is rebuked, that no one may think another unworthy to be taught by him what he knows not.

*His eyes being opened. ((RAB.))* There is shown to him in the body what he suffered before in the soul. For as an eye is open without sight, so the law is useless without the faith of Christ.

((BEDA.)) He could not with his eyes see well again, unless first blinded, and shutting out his own wisdom, which is troubled , he committed himself to the faith.

*And he was. ((RAB.))* Here a form is given to penitents, that they begin from a space of three days, and in this three days' space also the degree of the catechumens is dedicated.

*Three days.* It appears that through the three days, being blinded, he was awaiting the light of grace, not growing sluggish in idleness, but, enlightened by God, he was searching into heavenly things. It is credible that even at that time he was fully taught the dispensation of the Gospel.

*Not seeing.* Because he did not believe that God, rising on the third day, had overcome death, he is instructed by his own example, who changed the darkness of the three days by the returning light.

*He did not eat. ((RAB.))* This had befallen his soul, which had not had the inward food and drink. But from the fasting of the body and from thirst it is shown that the needy soul must be filled.
*Ananias. ((ID.))* It is a sign of familiarity that one is called by his own name.
*Into the village. ((ID.))* Villages are called lands lying next either to cities, or to one another within a city.
*Go,* etc. He is not to be feared as a persecutor, but to be embraced as a brother: because the evils which he brought upon the saints, he is ready to endure.
*He entered in.* The prophecy of Isaias was fulfilled, who says: *The wolf shall dwell with the lamb,* that is, Saul with Ananias.

*There fell,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The body of the serpent is covered with scales, etc., *as far as* that he received light in the mind.

((RAB.)) That the scales fall is a likeness of the inward sight renewed from the veil of the law.
*And immediately.* He fulfils the word of the Lord who says: *He that will come after me, let him deny himself ((Luc. IX))*, etc.

notes.text: Cometh — Speedily and in due season.
Mountain — My kingdom: kingdoms are usually called mountains in prophetical writings.
Profit — What wilt thou gain by it? The dust - Shall they that are dead celebrate thy goodness in the land of the living? Or, shall my dust praise thee?

Sackcloth — Given me occasion to put off that sackcloth, which they used to wear in times of mourning, Esth iv, 1 chap. xxxv, 13 Isaiah xxxii, 11 Joel i, 13. Girded - With joy, as with a garment, surrounding me on every side.

My glory — My tongue. David professes his confidence in God, intermixing prayer to him, ver. 1-8. Complains to God and prays for deliverance, ver. 9-18. Concludes with giving glory to God, and encouraging others to trust him, ver. 19-24. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *O Lord my God, I have cried to thee,* etc. ((AUG.)) Christ, etc., *as far as* but not in the dedication.
*Into the pit.* ((HIER.)) That is, out of the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, lest, like them, I should fall headlong into death.
*Confess ye,* etc. ((AUG.)) Because out of his own goodness and holiness, not ours, he was mindful of us.

*For wrath.* ((ID.)) That is, vengeance, by which he avenged upon us the first sin, which by death you have loosed.

*At evening.* ((ID.)) Because wrath, etc., *as far as* that is, in the time of grace after the time before the law and under the law.

((HIER.)) *At evening.* Because, when the Lord had suffered and been buried, the Apostles and the women continued in weeping and groaning. *And in the morning gladness.* Because coming to the sepulchre in the morning they received from the Angels the glory of the resurrection. *Weeping.* ((CASS.)) It shall abide for men who look toward the evening, at which Adam turned aside and went out from paradise: but there shall be gladness for those who look toward the morning, at which Christ rose again.

*But I.* How he acted before the dedication and deserved it. ((AUG., CASS.)) He acts at evening. But I, while abundance was mine in paradise, said: I shall not be moved from this good, believing the devil who said: *Thou shalt not die the death ((Gen. III))* . But, O Lord, in *thy will thou hast given strength to my beauty;* which is, I was good and strong not of myself, but of thee. And that thou mightest show it: *Thou hast turned away thy face,* that is, thou hast sent me forth out of paradise: but now, set here, *I will cry to thee,* etc.

*Thou hast turned away.* ((CASS.)) God turned away his face from Christ, by exposing him to the passion and to death; and thus Christ was troubled: *My soul is sorrowful even unto death. ((Matth. XVI.)) Troubled.* ((AUG.)) Calling to mind that time of trouble and of misery, and set in it, I hear the voice of the head who is to die for me, saying: *To thee, O Lord, will I cry.*

*What profit is there in my blood.* ((ID.)) He shows the necessity by which he does not suffer him to go down into corruption. *Whilst I go down into corruption.* For if I do not rise again at once, and the body is corrupted, I shall announce to no one, I shall gain no one. Confession is twofold, let us never be without it: when it is ill with us in tribulations, let us confess our sins; when it is well, let us confess praise to God in the exultation of justice.
*The Lord hath heard.* ((CASS.)) He treats of how he received it, namely the dedication. He said: I will cry, I will beseech, but the Lord heard me beseeching.

*Thou hast cut my sackcloth.* ((ID.)) Sackcloth is a rough garment, granted for the use of labour or in a time of sadness, as to the Ninivites; that is, human flesh, which was rent by dying: and there came forth the corn of the glorious resurrection, or of the godhead. Or else, the penalty of sin, which being destroyed in the resurrection, the godhead before hidden was brought forth: just as what the sack conceals whole, it opens when rent. ((AUG.)) Sackcloth of goats or of kids is mortality, which Christ drew or took from sinners; whence: *Whilst they were troublesome to me, I was clothed with haircloth ((Psal. XXXIV))*, that they might not see what was within.
*I shall not be pricked.* ((ID.)) I shall not now die unto the end. *O Lord God, I will confess to thee for ever.* What is: *I will confess to thee for ever?* For ever I will praise thee.

notes.text: And I saw — The many angels. And heard - The voice and the number of them. Round about the elders - So forming the third circle. It is remarkable, that men are represented through this whole vision as nearer to God than any of the angels. And the number of them was - At least two hundred millions, and two millions over. And yet these were but a part of the holy angels. Afterward, chap. vii, 11, St. John heard them all.

Worthy is the Lamb — The elders said, ver. 9, "Worthy art thou." They were more nearly allied to him than the angels. To receive the power, &c. - This sevenfold applause answers the seven seals, of which the four former describe all visible, the latter all invisible, things, made subject to the Lamb. And every one of these seven words bears a resemblance to the seal which it answers.

And every creature — In the whole universe, good or bad. In the heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea - With these four regions of the world, agrees the fourfold word of praise. What is in heaven, says blessing; what is on earth, honour; what is under the earth, glory: what is on the sea, strength; is unto him. This praise from all creatures begins before the opening of the first seal; but it continues from that time to eternity, according to the capacity of each. His enemies must acknowledge his glory; but those in heaven say, Blessed be God and the Lamb. This royal manifesto is, as it were, a proclamation, showing how Christ fulfils all things, and "every knee bows to him," not only on earth, but also in heaven, and under the earth. This book exhausts all things, 1 Cor. xv, 27, 28, and is suitable to an heart enlarged as the sand of the sea. It inspires the attentive and intelligent reader with such a magnanimity, that he accounts nothing in this world great; no, not the whole frame of visible nature, compared to the immense greatness of what he is here called to behold, yea, and in part, to inherit. St. John has in view, through the whole following vision, what he has been now describing, namely, the four living creatures, the elders, the angels, and all creatures, looking together at the opening of the seven seals. The seven seals are not distinguished from each other by specifying the time of them. They swiftly follow the letters to the seven churches, and all begin almost at the same time. By the four former is shown, that all the public occurrences of all ages and nations, as empire, war, provision, calamities, are made subject to Christ. And instances are intimated of the first in the east, the second in the west, the third in the south, the fourth in the north and the whole world. The contents, as of the phials and trumpets, so of the seals, are shown by the songs of praise and thanksgiving annexed to them. They contain therefore "the power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing," which the Lamb received. The four former have a peculiar connection with each other; and so have the three latter seals. The former relate to visible things, toward the four quarters to which the four living creatures look. Before we proceed, it may be observed,

glossa.text:
*I saw.* Not only the living creatures and the elders bearing the same witness out of their office, but also *I heard,*

 *The voice of angels.* That is, of the supernal spirits who fortify and guard the Church, who rejoice over the restored fellowship of the saints, who bear witness to Christ, and who both at his nativity, when they appeared to the shepherds, and at his passion, and at his resurrection and ascension, testified that the judge would come. Or the angels are the lesser subjects in the Church, leading an angelic life, who surround and honour their preachers and their judges, consenting to their testimony and conforming themselves to it. *Of many round about the throne and of the living creatures and of the elders,* etc. The more they are, the greater the attestation, and the greater the joy. *Thousands of thousands.* He set down this number, because that is finite with God which to men is infinite.
*Wisdom, and strength,* etc. The knowledge of all things, even as the Word united to himself has it.

*Benediction.* That is, the increase which we have in good works, *and honour* which follows therefrom, *and glory* from the virtues which we receive in baptism, *and power* by which we resist concupiscences, let it be attributed not to us, but to thee.

*And the four living creatures.* All the elders and the living creatures give their assent to the testimony of the angels. *They fell upon their faces,* etc. They are not proud because they judge others, but they humble themselves.

notes.text: There were together — At home, in one house.
They knew not that it was Jesus — Probably their eyes were holden.

They were not able to draw it for the multitude of fishes — This was not only a demonstration of the power of our Lord, but a kind supply for them and their families, and such as might be of service to them, when they waited afterward in Jerusalem. It was likewise an emblem of the great success which should attend them as fishers of men.

Peter girt on his upper coat (for he was stript of it before) — Reverencing the presence of his Lord: and threw himself into the sea - To swim to him immediately. The love of Christ draws men through fire and water.
Come ye and dine — Our Lord needed not food. And none presumed - To ask a needless question.
The third time — That he appeared to so many of the apostles together.

Simon, son of Jonah — The appellation Christ had given him, when be made that glorious confession, Matt. xvi, 16, the remembrance of which might make him more deeply sensible of his late denial of him whom he had so confessed. Lovest thou me? - Thrice our Lord asks him, who had denied him thrice: more than these - Thy fellow disciples do? - Peter thought so once, Matt. xxvi, 33, but he now answers only- I love thee, without adding more than these. Thou knowest - He had now learnt by sad experience that Jesus knew his heart. My lambs - The weakest and tenderest of the flock.
Because he said the third time — As if he did not believe him.

When thou art old — He lived about thirty-six years after this: another shall gird thee - They were tied to the cross till the nails were driven in; and shall carry thee - With the cross: whither thou wouldest not - According to nature; to the place where the cross was set up.
By what death he should glorify God — It is not only by acting, but chiefly by suffering, that the saints glorify God. Follow me - Showing hereby likewise what death he should die.

glossa.text: *Afterwards he manifested.* Having left all things they had followed Jesus. But if after the death of Jesus, before he was restored to them alive, they had taken up their former craft again, they might seem to have done this out of despair; but after he was restored alive, after they had received the spirit of his breathing, after his words: *As the Father hath sent me, I also send you,* suddenly they become what they had been, fishers, not of men but of fishes. But it is to be known that they were not forbidden to seek their living by their own lawful craft, the integrity of the apostolate being preserved, since they had not whereof to live; and so, as they laboured, God added the necessary things which he had promised; but here their want was disposed, that in the fishing such great sacraments might be displayed.

*This now.* Not that he was manifested only three times, but he refers it to the days: on the first day, on which he rose again; after eight days; on this day, when he did this concerning the fishes. The manifestations therefore are numbered according to the days. The first, however often it was made, on the one day of the resurrection. The second, after eight days; and this is the third. In this third manifestation this Gospel is ended.

*When therefore they had dined.* Jesus knows what he asks, whether he loves more; Peter says what he knows of himself, that is, that he loves. And because he does not know concerning the others how much they love, therefore he is silent as to whether he loves more than they. Behold, he teaches not to determine rashly about hidden things; and by the earlier peril of his denial he answers of himself more cautiously.

*Feed my lambs.* If thou love me, *feed my lambs.* Not as thine own: seek my glory in them, not thine own; my gains, not thine, because the love of God is proved in the love of the neighbour. But he who denies the work of piety to his neighbours loves God less. And this charity is given out of divine grace. Which John silently hints at when, asking about love, he says here what he does not say elsewhere: *Simon, son of John,* that is, obedient by the grace of God, because that he loves and obeys more ardently than the rest is nothing save the grace of God.

*He saith to him the third time.* He asks what he knew, not once, but again and a third time; and a third time he hears from Peter that he is loved, and a third time he bids him feed the sheep. To the threefold denial a threefold confession is rendered, lest the tongue serve love less than fear. And as it was the judgment of fear to deny the shepherd, so it is the office of love to feed the Lord's flock. *Peter was grieved. ((AUG.))* Even when his sins are forgiven a man endures the misery into which nevertheless he came out of sin. For the punishment is drawn out longer than the fault, and the fault would seem no small thing if the punishment were taken away along with it. It is therefore either for the showing of the misery that is owed, or for the amending of a slipping life, or for the exercise of necessary patience, that punishment holds a man for a time, even him whom guilt no longer holds as guilty; and this is the condition of these days, to be wept over, but not to be blamed. *Feed.* To feed the sheep is to comfort believers lest they fail, to provide earthly supports, if it be necessary, for those subject to one, to offer examples of the virtues, to withstand adversaries, to correct those who sin.

*But when thou shalt be old.* He foretells that he will suffer, who had foretold that he would deny; strengthened by the resurrection he could now do that which, while weak, he promised before its time. Now he does not fear the ending of this life, because, the Lord rising again, the example of another life went before.

*And when he had said this.* These things being said, Jesus began to go away; and, not yet understanding what he had heard, *Follow me,* Peter began to follow with the going of his feet; and John also followed, who knew that he was loved.

echoes.text: I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision; but a great quaking fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves. So I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me; for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength. Yet heard I the voice of his words; and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I fallen into a deep sleep on my face, with my face […]
echoes.note: Daniel alone perceives the vision while the men with him do not see it but flee in terror; he then falls to the ground. Acts 9:7's companions 'stood speechless, hearing the sound but seeing no one' is the same selective-perception convention attached to an overwhelming theophany, with the seer prostrate. Volume and thematic coherence are strong; the divergence (companions hear vs. do not see) is exactly the kind of variation Luke replays in his retellings (cf. ch. 22, 26).

echoes.text: As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.
echoes.note: The appearance of the glory of the LORD as radiant brightness causes Ezekiel to fall on his face and hear a voice speaking. Saul's 'light from the sky,' falling to the earth, and a speaking voice replays the Kavod-theophany sequence. High thematic coherence with the prophetic call pattern; verbal volume is moderate (light/glory, fell, voice).

echoes.text: He said to me, Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you. The Spirit entered into me when he spoke to me, and set me on my feet; and I heard him who spoke to me. He said to me, Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me even to this very day.
echoes.note: After Ezekiel falls, the voice commands 'Son of man, stand on your feet... I send you to the people.' Saul is told to 'rise up, and enter into the city,' the same fall-then-rise-and-go commissioning rhythm. Coherence with the immediately following sending to the nations is strong; verbal borrowing modest.

echoes.text: When Yahweh saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the midst of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!” He said, “Here I am.”
echoes.note: 'Moses, Moses' — the doubled-vocative call from a blazing divine manifestation, answered before commission. 'Saul, Saul' matches the convention. Recurrence is strong across the OT call type-scenes (Gen 22:11; 46:2; 1 Sam 3:10), which strengthens rather than dilutes the echo.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was […]
echoes.note: The throne-vision call of Isaiah — overwhelmed prophet confronted by divine glory, then sent — is the archetype Luke draws Saul's commissioning into. Little verbal overlap, but the type-scene logic (theophany → unworthiness → sending) is the figural frame; coherence high, volume low.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: Jeremiah is appointed 'a prophet to the nations' before birth; the Damascus call culminates (v.15) in Saul as the chosen vessel 'before the nations.' The conversion proper carries this only faintly; the nations-prophet resonance lands more in vv.10-19. Low volume here.

echoes.text: When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. Now terror and great darkness fell on him.
echoes.note: A dread/darkness falls upon Abram at a covenant theophany; Saul is plunged into three days of darkness. Faint, contested — the motif of incapacitating darkness accompanying divine encounter, but no verbal contact.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Damascus
places.id: On the Barada river east of the Anti-Lebanon mountains, one of the longest continuously inhabited cities in the world. The Aramean capital of the Iron Age (1 Kgs 11:24), Hellenistic Damascus, in the apostolic period under Nabataean influence (cf. 2 Cor 11:32-33) but within the Roman provincial framework. The 'street called Straight' (Decumanus Maximus) of 9:11 still runs east-west through the Old City.

echoes.text: A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
echoes.note: Hays: high — 'ten thousands of ten thousands, and thousands of thousands' is a near-verbatim adoption of Daniel's heavenly-court formula 'thousands of thousands... ten thousand times ten thousand' attending the Ancient of Days. John relocates this innumerable angelic host around the throne and the Lamb. The shared context (heavenly throne-room, opened books/sealed scroll) makes this the controlling intertext for 5:11. LXX/Theodotion 'chiliai chiliades... myriai myriades' matches Revelation's wording.

echoes.text: Praise Yahweh from the earth, you great sea creatures, and all depths! Lightning and hail, snow and clouds; stormy wind, fulfilling his word; mountains and all hills; fruit trees and all cedars; wild animals and all livestock; small creatures and flying birds; kings of the earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of the earth; both young men and maidens; old men and children: let them praise Yahweh’s name, for his name alone is exalted. His glory is […]
echoes.note: Hays: high — 'every created thing which is in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea' enacts the cosmic, totalizing praise of Psalm 148, which summons every creature of heaven, earth, and sea to praise. John structures the doxology by the same heaven/earth/sea/under-earth merism. The universal sweep of creation's worship is the Psalm's signature.

echoes.text: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.
echoes.note: Hays: high — the sevenfold acclamation 'power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing' and the doxology 'blessing, honor, glory, and dominion' draw on David's catalogue of divine attributes ('the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, the majesty... the kingdom'). The piling of abstract honors ascribed to God — now jointly to God and the Lamb — patterns on this temple-dedication doxology. Reinforces the worthiness language of 4:11; 7:12.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Hays: medium — the ascription of 'the dominion, forever and ever' to the one on the throne and the Lamb echoes Daniel's grant of everlasting 'dominion' and 'glory' to the son of man. Pairs with Dan 7:10 in 5:11; the same chapter supplies both the angelic myriads and the eternal dominion that frame the doxology's climax.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: Hays: low / contested — Second Temple apocalyptic (1 Enoch 39:12–40:1; 60:1; 71:8) shares Revelation's scene of innumerable angelic myriads ceaselessly blessing the enthroned Lord, suggesting a common throne-vision milieu rather than direct dependence. Daniel 7:10 remains the canonical source. Included to register the Enochic background of the angelic-host doxology; not available in WEB, hence marked deuterocanonical/low.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: It shall happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, shall live; and there shall be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the river comes. It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's temple river makes the sea teem with fish 'of every kind,' with fishermen spreading nets from Engedi to Eneglaim. John's miraculous catch of fish 'of every kind' (the 153 traditionally read as the count of fish species) and the unbroken net coheres with Ezekiel's eschatological ingathering. Volume is moderate but the thematic coherence (river/sea, abundance, fishing, no-loss) is strong; contested but widely proposed.

echoes.text: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: The mandate to subdue and have dominion over 'the fish of the sea' lurks behind a restored humanity gathering the fish at the creative word of the risen Lord. Faint: shared lexeme 'fish of the sea' and a new-creation framing (resurrection 'after these things'), but no verbal citation and the link is thematic.

echoes.text: Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, to be sufficient for them? Shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, to be sufficient for them?”
echoes.note: Moses asks whether all the fish of the sea could be gathered to feed the people; John presents an answering abundance gathered by Jesus' word. Faint association on the motif of impossible provision of fish answered by divine sufficiency; offered only as a contested resonance.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: Peter is addressed as 'Simon, son of Jonah' (vv.15-17) amid a sea/fish narrative; the Jonah-the-prophet sea imagery may color the scene of disciples on the deep at night. Faint and largely onomastic; included honestly as contested.

echoes.text: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. They heard the voice of Yahweh God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden. Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I […]
echoes.note: Peter, 'naked,' covers himself before encountering the Lord (v.7), recalling the shame/covering of Eden when the man hid from the LORD's presence. Faint verbal touch ('naked') with a coherent theme of standing exposed before the divine; contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: The LORD appears and a meal is set before him/by him; here the risen Lord hosts a theophanic breakfast none dare question. Faint typological resonance of divine appearance plus prepared food; coherence with John's revelation motif ('revealed himself') but no verbal anchor.

echoes.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty […]
echoes.note: Elijah, exhausted, is given bread baked on coals by the LORD's messenger and strengthened for the journey; Jesus provides bread and fish from a charcoal fire to strengthen the disciples for mission. Faint but coherent provision-meal-after-failure motif; contested.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.
echoes.note: God promises to set up 'one shepherd' to feed and tend the flock. Jesus' triple charge to Peter—'feed my lambs / tend my sheep / feed my sheep'—delegates this messianic shepherd office. High volume of shepherd language, strong coherence with Johannine 'good shepherd' (ch.10), and clear availability in Ezekiel 34's feed/tend vocabulary.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
echoes.note: The LORD as shepherd who feeds and leads the flock supplies the foundational pastoral imagery taken up in the commission to feed and tend sheep. Coherent and available, though general; the verbal link is thematic (shepherd/feed) rather than a citation.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: Against false shepherds who scatter, God will raise shepherds who 'feed' the flock so none is missing. Peter's reinstatement as a true shepherd who feeds coheres tightly with Jeremiah's contrast; moderate volume in shared feed/shepherd vocabulary.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The LORD 'will feed his flock like a shepherd' and gently carry the lambs—matching the specific pairing of lambs and sheep in Peter's threefold charge. Strong coherence and the distinctive lamb/sheep doublet raise volume above the generic shepherd topos.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses asks God to appoint a successor so the congregation is not 'as sheep without a shepherd'; Joshua is commissioned over the flock. Jesus' commissioning of Peter to shepherd reprises this succession-of-shepherd pattern; coherent with the leadership-transfer theme of John 21.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: The prophet is told to 'feed the flock' destined for slaughter, foreshadowing a shepherd's costly office immediately before Peter's death-prophecy (vv.18-19). Faint but coherent given the adjoining martyrdom prediction; contested.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: The thrice-repeated 'Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?' echoes the testing/love idiom of the Aqedah where God names the beloved son in a graduated demand. Faint structural resonance (threefold address, love, testing); offered as contested.

echoes.text: I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts;
echoes.note: 'I have stretched out my hands all day long' supplies a possible scriptural backdrop for 'you will stretch out your hands,' read by early Christians as crucifixion imagery. Faint verbal touch ('stretch out hands'); coherent with the death-prophecy but contested as the source.

echoes.text: My eyes are dim from grief. I have called on you daily, Yahweh. I have spread out my hands to you.
echoes.note: The afflicted 'spread out my hands' to God in a context of approaching death; resonates with Peter's foretold death by stretched-out hands and being led where he does not wish. Faint, generic gesture-language; contested.

echoes.text: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw near, when you will say, “I have no pleasure in them”;
echoes.note: Qoheleth's contrast of youth and the days of trouble in old age frames the 'when you were young... when you are old' antithesis of Peter's prophecy. Faint thematic parallel of life-stage contrast; offered as contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
They fished all night and caught nothing,
and at daybreak a voice from the shore filled the nets.
You turned our mourning into dancing;
by the charcoal fire he asked, Do you love me? Then feed my sheep.
Come and have breakfast, the risen Lord says.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Stand on the shore in the gray of early morning, your nets empty, your arms tired from a long and fruitless night.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
A figure on the beach calls out, cast the net again — and it comes up so full it will not break.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
There is a charcoal fire going, and fish on it, and bread, and the smell of breakfast drifts across the water: Come and eat.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
By that same fire he asks the question three times over: Do you love me? Then feed my sheep.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
You turned our weeping into dancing; we come to the fire to be fed and sent:
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The nets are empty, the long night gone.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
A voice from the shore fills them to breaking.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Bread and fish on the fire: Come and have breakfast.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Do you love me? Feed my sheep. Come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
